title: Day 9X — I2C: Two Wires, and a Display That Works

slides.title: I2C: A Two-Wire Bus
slides.subtitle: ENGS 28 · Day 9X — In-Class

slides.title: Where we are
items: Nothing from Tuesday is a prerequisite for today. No EXTI, no NVIC, no ISR, no volatile — this is a new peripheral and a new protocol.
Two habits carry over: go to the reference manual for a number rather than guessing it, and assign a whole mask to a control register rather than compound-assigning one bit into it.
In the first twelve minutes we wire a display to two of the Nucleo's pins, flash a program you are given, and read four characters off it.
Everything after that answers the question you then have: how did two wires do that?
slides.presenterNote: ≈ 2 min with announcements. 50-minute session — say the shape out loud, because the payoff lands early today rather than late.

Recap
items: Two wires, shared by everything on them: a clock the controller drives, and a data line every device can pull LOW and none can drive HIGH.
A transaction is START, seven address bits, the R/W bit, an ACK from whoever recognized the address, data bytes each with their own ACK, and a STOP. You have one on a screen with your name on it.
What you #define is always the 7-bit address. The library shifts it, which is why the wire carries 0xE0 where your program says 0x70.
A digit's byte is 0b DP g f e d c b a, and the display buffer is two bytes per position — digits at 0, 2, 6 and 8, the colon at 4.
No new homework tonight — Tuesday's timer program is what is due. Leave the display wired.
Two debts to collect tomorrow: what i2c1_byteWrite() and i2c1_memWrite() actually do, and where those three command bytes came from.
